What the QR code test checks

A QR code that scans on your screen can still fail on a small sticker or a worn menu. The tester runs the same code through several harder conditions and tells you how it did.

  • Decodes at full size: the basic test. Can the code be read at all?
  • Decodes when shrunk: half, quarter and very small versions, to imitate small print sizes and distance.
  • Decodes when slightly blurred, like a phone that has not focused well (where your browser supports it).
  • Dark on light: flags inverted codes that some scanners cannot read.
  • Contrast: estimates the contrast between the dark and light modules.
  • Content length: long content makes a denser code that needs more space.

The result is a guide. Real-world scanning depends on the phone, lighting, print quality and surface, so still try the printed code on real phones.

How to test a QR code before printing

A short routine avoids costly reprints.

  1. Export your QR code as an image (PNG or SVG converted to PNG) or take a screenshot.
  2. Upload it or paste it into the tester above and read the verdict and the checklist.
  3. Fix any warnings: raise contrast, shorten the link, or plan a larger print size.
  4. Print a test copy at the real size and scan it with at least two different phones (an iPhone and an Android).
  5. Test it in the place where it will hang, with the real lighting and at a normal scanning distance.

QR code size and scanning distance

As a rough guide, the code should be about one tenth of the scanning distance. These are starting points, not guarantees.

Where it is scannedTypical distanceSuggested minimum size
Business card or receiptAbout 20 cm (8 in)About 2 cm (0.8 in)
Menu or table tentAbout 30 cm (12 in)About 3 cm (1.2 in)
Poster or shop window1 to 2 m (3 to 6 ft)10 to 20 cm (4 to 8 in)
Billboard or banner5 m and more50 cm (20 in) and more

Common reasons a QR code fails

These come up again and again.

  • Too small for the distance, especially with dense, long content.
  • Low contrast, such as light gray on white, or a busy image behind the code.
  • Inverted colors (light code on a dark background).
  • No quiet zone. The blank margin around the code was cropped or covered.
  • Oversized logo in the middle that hides too much of the pattern.
  • Glossy or curved surface that reflects light or distorts the code.
  • Wrong or outdated link. The code scans, but the page is missing.
